lessonTitle: Pool and Flow Boiling: Regimes and Critical Heat Flux

blocks.text: A 12 kW immersion heater boils water in a laboratory tank without trouble for months, then one day the tank level drops, the element glows red and the sheath melts within seconds. Nothing about the power setting changed. The heater crossed the critical heat flux, and this unit explains why that boundary is so abrupt and so destructive.

blocks.markdown: **Pool boiling** is boiling on a heated surface submerged in a large stagnant volume of liquid, so all fluid motion is driven by buoyancy of the vapour bubbles themselves. The surface is at $T_s$, the liquid is at its saturation temperature $T_{sat}$, and the driving temperature difference is the **excess temperature** $\Delta T_e = T_s - T_{sat}$ (in K). The surface heat flux $q''$ (in W/m$^2$) is plotted against $\Delta T_e$ to give the **boiling curve** first measured by Nukiyama in 1934.

blocks.title: Critical heat flux (CHF)
blocks.text: The critical heat flux $q''_{max}$ is the maximum heat flux that nucleate boiling can carry. Beyond it so much vapour leaves the surface that liquid can no longer reach it, and the surface is blanketed by vapour.

blocks.markdown: Walk along the boiling curve for saturated water at 1 atm, increasing $\Delta T_e$. At small excess temperature (below about 5 K) there are no bubbles and heat leaves by **natural convection**. Bubbles then form at surface cavities, first as isolated bubbles and then as jets and columns: this is **nucleate boiling**, with very high heat transfer coefficients because bubble growth and departure stir the thin liquid layer. At the peak of the curve the flux reaches $q''_{max}$. Further increase in $\Delta T_e$ makes vapour patches appear and collapse, so the flux **falls**: this is **transition boiling** (unstable partial film boiling). At the minimum (the Leidenfrost point) a stable vapour film forms; in **film boiling** the flux rises again, now through a low-conductivity vapour layer plus radiation.

rows: Alternating vapour patches and liquid contact
Continuous vapour blanket, conduction and radiation
blocks.caption: Regimes on the pool boiling curve; the temperature ranges are typical values for water and vary with surface and pressure.

blocks.markdown: For saturated pool boiling on a large flat horizontal surface, a hydrodynamic argument (Zuber; his original constant is 0.131, which this unit uses, and Lienhard and Dhir later refined it to about 0.149) balances the buoyant escape of vapour against the liquid that must flow in to replace it. The result is the standard CHF correlation, with all properties at saturation.

blocks.caption: Zuber correlation with his original constant $C=0.131$ (Lienhard and Dhir refined it to about 0.149); $h_{fg}$ latent heat (J/kg), $\rho_l,\rho_v$ liquid and vapour densities (kg/m$^3$), $\sigma$ surface tension (N/m), $g$ gravity (m/s$^2$)

blocks.title: CHF of saturated water at 1 atm
blocks.prompt: Estimate the critical heat flux for saturated water at 1 atm on a large horizontal plate. Typical properties: $h_{fg}=2257$ kJ/kg, $\rho_l=957.9$ kg/m$^3$, $\rho_v=0.5956$ kg/m$^3$, $\sigma=0.0589$ N/m, $g=9.81$ m/s$^2$.

steps.text: Compute the buoyancy-surface-tension group, using $\rho_l-\rho_v=957.3$ kg/m$^3$.

blocks.answer: $q''_{max}\approx 1.1$ MW/m$^2$, in line with measured values near 1 MW/m$^2$ for clean water at atmospheric pressure.

blocks.markdown: Why does CHF matter so much in practice? Many heaters are **heat-flux-controlled**: an electric resistance element or a nuclear fuel rod releases a fixed power per unit area regardless of its own temperature. Surfaces cooled by a hot fluid, by contrast, are **temperature-controlled** because the wall temperature is set by the fluid. The difference decides what happens at the peak of the boiling curve.

blocks.title: Why burnout happens at CHF
blocks.text: On a heat-flux-controlled surface the heat generated is fixed at $q''$. If $q''$ is raised slightly above $q''_{max}$, nucleate boiling cannot remove it, so the surface heats up. Moving along the curve to larger $\Delta T_e$ would make the removable flux fall (transition boiling), so the surface keeps heating until it reaches the film-boiling branch where the removable flux again equals the generated flux. That intersection can be hundreds of kelvin hotter, often above the melting point of the material: this is **burnout**.

blocks.title: Maximum safe power of a heater
blocks.prompt: A flat horizontal heater face measures 0.020 m by 0.500 m and is immersed in saturated water at 1 atm with $q''_{max}=1.107$ MW/m$^2$. Find the maximum power at CHF and the power at a design limit of 70 % of CHF.

steps.text: Power at CHF equals CHF times area.
Apply the 70 % design factor, so the heater stays in the nucleate regime with margin for imperfect surface condition.

blocks.answer: At CHF the face can carry 11.1 kW; a 12 kW heater on this face would burn out, and the safe design power is about 7.7 kW.

items: Raising system pressure changes $h_{fg}$, $\rho_v$ and $\sigma$ together; for water, CHF rises with pressure at moderate pressures and peaks at roughly one third of the critical pressure.
CHF scales as $g^{1/4}$, so reduced gravity lowers it only modestly.
Subcooled liquid and forced flow raise CHF; fouled or heavily oxidised surfaces change nucleation but the hydrodynamic limit is similar.
The correlation applies to large, clean, flat, horizontal surfaces; small cylinders and spheres need modified constants.

blocks.title: Do not control power near CHF
blocks.text: Operating a heat-flux-controlled surface close to $q''_{max}$ leaves no margin: a slight rise in power, a lower liquid level or a fall in pressure can trigger burnout. Real designs apply a safety factor (commonly 0.5 to 0.8 of the predicted CHF).

points: The pool boiling curve has natural convection, nucleate, transition and film regimes; the flux peaks at CHF and has a minimum at the Leidenfrost point.
CHF for saturated pool boiling is estimated with $q''_{max}=0.131h_{fg}\rho_v^{1/2}[\sigma g(\rho_l-\rho_v)]^{1/4}$.
On a heat-flux-controlled surface, exceeding CHF forces a jump to film boiling at a very high wall temperature, which is the cause of burnout.
Design below CHF with a margin, and remember the correlation assumes a clean, large, horizontal, saturated surface.

questions.stem: A thin plate is boiling saturated water at atmospheric pressure with a measured wall temperature 60 K above saturation, in a test where wall temperature is held fixed by a thermostatic bath. Using the typical regime ranges in the lesson, which regime is most likely present?

options.text: Nucleate boiling, because the bubbles are still attached to cavities at this temperature
Transition boiling, because the excess temperature is beyond the heat-flux peak and the flux falls as it rises
Stable film boiling, because any excess temperature above 30 K gives a vapour blanket
Natural convection, because the liquid is at saturation

questions.correctOptionText: Transition boiling, because the excess temperature is beyond the heat-flux peak and the flux falls as it rises

distractorRationale.a: Typical nucleate boiling for water ends near 30 K of excess temperature, well below 60 K.
distractorRationale.c: The stable film regime typically starts above about 120 K of excess temperature, not 30 K.
distractorRationale.d: Natural convection is limited to roughly the first 5 K of excess temperature; at 60 K bubbles and vapour patches dominate.

questions.explanation: Between roughly 30 K and 120 K of excess temperature, water at 1 atm lies on the transition branch, where vapour patches form and collapse and the heat flux decreases as the wall gets hotter. Because the wall temperature is held fixed here, this normally unstable regime can be observed and measured.

questions.stem: Which description fits film boiling on the pool boiling curve?

options.text: Discrete bubbles grow at surface cavities and carry latent heat away in jets
Buoyant liquid motion alone removes heat, with no bubbles forming
A continuous vapour blanket separates the surface from the liquid, so heat crosses a low-conductivity layer and radiation becomes important
Vapour patches repeatedly form and collapse so the heat flux increases with excess temperature

questions.correctOptionText: A continuous vapour blanket separates the surface from the liquid, so heat crosses a low-conductivity layer and radiation becomes important

distractorRationale.a: That describes nucleate boiling, where the liquid still wets the surface.
distractorRationale.b: That is the natural convection region at very small excess temperature.
distractorRationale.d: Alternating patches are transition boiling, where the flux decreases, not increases, with excess temperature.

questions.explanation: In film boiling the surface is so hot that liquid cannot touch it, and a stable vapour layer forms. Vapour conducts poorly, so a large temperature difference is needed for a given flux, and radiation across the film adds to the heat transfer at high wall temperatures.

questions.stem: On the pool boiling curve for water the heat flux increases continuously as the excess temperature increases from the onset of nucleate boiling all the way into the film boiling regime.
questions.explanation: The curve rises to a maximum at CHF, then falls through transition boiling to a minimum at the Leidenfrost point before rising again in film boiling. The dip is the reason a heat-flux-controlled surface cannot follow the curve beyond the peak and instead jumps.

questions.stem: A heater in saturated ethanol at 1 atm sits on a large horizontal plate. Use the Zuber correlation with C = 0.131 and typical properties: h_fg = 846 kJ/kg, liquid density 757 kg/m^3, vapour density 1.435 kg/m^3, surface tension 0.0177 N/m, g = 9.81 m/s^2. Find the critical heat flux in kW/m^2.
questions.explanation: Evaluate sqrt(1.435) = 1.198 and [0.0177 x 9.81 x (757-1.435)]^(1/4) = [131.2]^(1/4) = 3.384. Then q''max = 0.131 x 846000 x 1.198 x 3.384 = 449310 W/m^2, or about 449 kW/m^2. Ethanol has a much lower latent heat and surface tension than water, so its CHF is well below water's.

questions.stem: A short cylindrical heater of diameter 6.0 mm and length 150 mm is immersed in saturated liquid nitrogen at 1 atm. Treat the CHF as that of a large flat plate (Zuber, C = 0.131) and use typical properties: h_fg = 199 kJ/kg, liquid density 807 kg/m^3, vapour density 4.61 kg/m^3, surface tension 0.0089 N/m, g = 9.81 m/s^2. Taking the heated area as the curved side surface only, find the maximum power in W that the heater can dissipate before burnout.
questions.explanation: The flat-plate CHF is 0.131 x 199000 x sqrt(4.61) x [0.0089 x 9.81 x 802.4]^(1/4) = 161.9 kW/m^2. The side area is pi x 0.006 x 0.150 = 28.27 cm^2 (0.002827 m^2), so Q = 161933 x 0.002827 = 458 W. Above this power a power-controlled heater would burn out, so the answer is a ceiling, not an operating point.

questions.stem: A boiling experiment is moved from Earth gravity (9.81 m/s^2) to a lunar surface where g = 1.62 m/s^2, with the same liquid and heater. According to the Zuber correlation, the CHF becomes approximately

options.text: 64 % of its Earth value, because CHF scales with $g^{1/4}$
16.5 % of its Earth value, because CHF scales directly with $g$
41 % of its Earth value, because CHF scales with $g^{1/2}$
The same value, because latent heat and densities do not depend on gravity

questions.correctOptionText: 64 % of its Earth value, because CHF scales with $g^{1/4}$

distractorRationale.b: CHF depends on the one-quarter power of $g$, not on $g$ itself; a linear dependence would be a large over-estimate of the loss.
distractorRationale.d: Gravity enters the buoyancy term $g(\rho_l-\rho_v)$ inside the bracket, so CHF does change, though only weakly.

questions.explanation: The correlation contains $[\sigma g(\rho_l-\rho_v)]^{1/4}$, so the ratio of CHF values is $(g_{moon}/g_{earth})^{1/4}=(0.165)^{0.25}=0.637$. A six-fold fall in gravity therefore lowers CHF by only about a third, because of the weak quarter-power dependence.

questions.stem: An electrically heated rod in saturated water is operated at constant electrical power per unit area that is increased slowly. When the power per unit area passes the critical heat flux, what is observed?

options.text: The surface temperature drops sharply because nucleate boiling becomes more vigorous
The surface temperature moves smoothly along the transition boiling curve to a new steady state
The heat flux removed rises further because more bubbles form
The surface temperature jumps to a very high value on the film boiling branch while the flux stays at the same applied value

questions.correctOptionText: The surface temperature jumps to a very high value on the film boiling branch while the flux stays at the same applied value

distractorRationale.a: Beyond CHF nucleate boiling cannot remove the heat, so the wall heats up rather than cools.
distractorRationale.b: On the transition branch the removable flux falls as temperature rises, so a flux-controlled surface cannot sit there steadily; it runs away.
distractorRationale.c: The removable flux in nucleate boiling is capped at CHF, which is why the surface cannot shed any extra power.

questions.explanation: The only steady state at a flux just above CHF is on the film boiling branch, so the wall temperature rises abruptly by hundreds of kelvin at essentially constant flux. Whether the heater survives depends on whether that temperature is below its melting point, which is why this event is called burnout.

questions.stem: State what physical limit sets the critical heat flux in saturated pool boiling, and explain qualitatively why an increase in surface tension and in $\rho_l - \rho_v$ both raise CHF while a larger latent heat does too.
markingGuide: CHF is a hydrodynamic limit: vapour leaves upward while liquid must flow downward to the surface; at CHF vapour columns/jets become unstable and liquid supply to the surface is choked
Heat flux is the product of vapour mass flux and latent heat, so larger $h_{fg}$ gives more heat for each kilogram of vapour that can escape
Larger $\rho_l-\rho_v$ increases buoyancy and counter-current liquid supply, raising the limiting vapour flux
Larger $\sigma$ stabilises the vapour-liquid interface against the instability and keeps the liquid wetting the surface
Reference to the form $q''_{max}\propto h_{fg}\rho_v^{1/2}[\sigma g(\rho_l-\rho_v)]^{1/4}$
questions.explanation: CHF is set by how much vapour can leave and liquid return, not by the heater material. Latent heat multiplies the escaping vapour flux, while buoyancy and surface tension stabilise the counter-flow, so each raises the limit as the correlation shows.

questions.stem: A designer proposes to test a small heater in boiling water first using a hot-oil bath that holds the wall at a chosen temperature, and then using electric heating at a chosen power. Explain why the first test can map the whole boiling curve but the second test can burn out the heater, using the shape of the boiling curve.
markingGuide: Identifies that a temperature-controlled surface fixes $\Delta T_e$, so each $\Delta T_e$ gives one $q''$ and the transition branch can be traversed steadily
Identifies that the electric heater is heat-flux-controlled: $q''$ is fixed and the wall temperature is the unknown
Notes the peak at CHF and the negative slope of $q''$ versus $\Delta T_e$ in transition boiling, so no steady state exists on that branch for a fixed flux
States that when $q''$ exceeds $q''_{max}$ the only intersecting steady branch is film boiling at a much higher wall temperature, giving a rapid temperature jump and possible melting
Mentions hysteresis: reducing power afterwards returns only at the lower Leidenfrost point flux
questions.explanation: The oil bath gives a one-to-one relation between wall temperature and flux, so the unstable negative-slope region is accessible. The electric heater fixes flux, so passing the peak leaves no nearby steady state except the very hot film boiling branch, which is the burnout transition.

questions.stem: A flat horizontal plate of area 0.050 m^2 dissipates 60 kW electrically into saturated water at 2 bar. Typical properties: h_fg = 2202 kJ/kg, liquid density 942.9 kg/m^3, vapour density 1.129 kg/m^3, surface tension 0.0550 N/m. Using the Zuber correlation (C = 0.131, g = 9.81 m/s^2), find the ratio of the critical heat flux to the applied heat flux (dimensionless safety factor).
questions.explanation: The applied flux is 60000/0.050 = 1.20 MW/m^2. The CHF is 0.131 x 2202000 x sqrt(1.129) x [0.0550 x 9.81 x 941.8]^(1/4) = 1.455 MW/m^2, so the ratio is 1.21. A factor of only about 1.2 is thin for a power-controlled surface, so a designer would reduce power or increase area to restore a larger margin.
